claims.text: Surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements governs the premelting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements governs the melting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed initial nanoparticles are equiatomic Cr-Co-Ni-Fe-Mn nanoparticles with a uniform elemental distribution.
Optimized rapid synthesis can minimize surface segregation in these nanoparticles.
Sub-melting-temperature annealing can induce surface segregation in these nanoparticles.
Heating drives redistribution that enriches nanoparticle surfaces in lower-melting-point components.
Differences in elemental melting points promote migration of lower-melting-point atoms to the nanoparticle surface as temperature increases.
Surface enrichment in lower-melting-point elements weakens local bonding.
The weakened local bonding caused by surface enrichment initiates premelting and lowers the effective melting point relative to a uniformly distributed nanoparticle.
Nanoparticles with induced surface segregation will begin premelting at a lower temperature than homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
The predicted reduction in premelting onset temperature is roughly 10–20%.
Nanoparticles with induced surface segregation will melt more gradually than homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with minimized surface segregation will exhibit a sharper melting transition.
Nanoparticles with minimized surface segregation will exhibit a higher premelting-onset temperature.
The proposed mechanism should apply to near-equimolar high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism should apply when heating does not cause phase decomposition or major structural transformations other than premelting.
The magnitude of the melting-temperature reduction and segregation effect depends on the elemental combination and processing conditions.
